articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Hungary’s parliament voted last Tuesday to repeal the 2021 Child Protection Law that banned the portrayal or promotion of homosexuality and transgender identities in schools and media. Within minutes, the EU announced it was releasing €4.2 billion (approximately $4.6 billion) in funds frozen over rule-of-law violations, a connection Budapest had been counting on.

From political weapon to political liability

Orbán’s government pushed the 2021 law as a child protection measure, framing gay and transgender people as a threat to public morals, and for years it worked. Then his government pardoned the deputy head of a children’s home convicted of covering up his boss’s child sexual abuse crimes, and what had been a political asset became the defining scandal of his final term.

Magyar ran his campaign on protecting children in state care and largely sidestepped the LGBTQ rights issue; his party needed conservative votes, and he was not going to risk alienating them.

Five years of legislation, unwound in one vote

Tuesday’s package went beyond the 2021 law, touching Fidesz-era changes to education policy and assembly rights. Civil rights group Háttér Society, which had been fighting the child protection law for five years, said most of the problems it had flagged in the draft had been fixed.

“We are very happy that this got adopted,” said Tamás Dombos of Háttér Society. “We’ve been fighting this so-called child protection law for five years.”

The repeal also cleared Hungary’s path to rejoin Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe, two major EU programs suspended during the Orbán years over rule-of-law violations. Tisza holds the same two-thirds parliamentary majority Orbán’s party once had, which meant the package passed without needing to negotiate.

Beyond the repeal

Háttér Society welcomed the vote, though the group was clear about how much remains unaddressed. It still wants full recognition of same-sex marriage, adoption rights for same-sex couples, and the right of transgender people to change their names on official documents, none of which are in the new legislation.

Magyar has been careful in how he frames the issue. “I’m very cautious,” he told Finnish daily Helsingin Sanomat. “As prime minister, it’s my duty to represent all Hungarians, and we have sensitive issues, such as the situation of sexual minorities.”

“We are still knocking on a closed door,” Dombos said, “but at least they are listening on the other side.” For a community that spent years being actively targeted, that is a real shift, even if full equality is still a long way off.

articles.personality_title: Hungary repeals anti-LGBTQ law, unlocking billions in EU funds
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In 2021, Hungary passed a law that banned showing or promoting LGBTQ identities in schools and media, claiming it was to protect children. This law caused strong criticism and led the European Union (EU) to freeze billions of euros in funds to Hungary.

**What happened** – Last Tuesday, Hungary’s parliament voted to cancel this 2021 law along with other related rules. Soon after, the EU announced it would release €4.2 billion (about $4.6 billion) in funds that had been frozen because of Hungary’s earlier actions.

**Impact** – This decision marks a big change for Hungary. It not only supports LGBTQ rights by removing a law seen as harmful but also allows Hungary to take part again in important EU programs like Erasmus+ (for student exchanges) and Horizon Europe (for research). It shows that political leaders are responding to public pressure and human rights concerns.

**What's next step** – Groups supporting LGBTQ rights say there is still work to do, including allowing same-sex marriage, adoption rights for same-sex couples, and legal recognition for transgender people. The new prime minister has promised to listen carefully to all citizens, which could lead to more progress in the future.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Hungary’s repeal of its anti-LGBTQ law ends years of discrimination and reopens access to billions in EU funds, signaling a hopeful step toward greater equality and cooperation.
articles.personality_title_fr: La Hongrie abroge une loi anti-LGBTQ et débloque des milliards de fonds européens
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En 2021, la Hongrie a adopté une loi interdisant la représentation ou la promotion des identités LGBTQ dans les écoles et les médias, sous prétexte de protéger les enfants. Cette loi a suscité de vives critiques et conduit l’Union européenne (UE) à geler plusieurs milliards d’euros de fonds destinés à la Hongrie.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Mardi dernier, le parlement hongrois a voté l’abrogation de cette loi de 2021 ainsi que d’autres règles connexes. Peu après, l’UE a annoncé la libération de 4,2 milliards d’euros (environ 4,6 milliards de dollars) de fonds qui avaient été gelés à cause des actions précédentes de la Hongrie.

**Impact** – Cette décision marque un grand changement pour la Hongrie. Elle soutient les droits LGBTQ en supprimant une loi considérée comme nuisible et permet à la Hongrie de participer à nouveau à des programmes importants de l’UE comme Erasmus+ (échanges étudiants) et Horizon Europe (recherche). Cela montre que les dirigeants politiques répondent aux pressions publiques et aux préoccupations liées aux droits humains.

**Prochaine étape** – Les groupes de défense des droits LGBTQ affirment qu’il reste des efforts à faire, notamment pour autoriser le mariage entre personnes de même sexe, les droits d’adoption pour ces couples, et la reconnaissance légale des personnes transgenres. Le nouveau Premier ministre a promis d’écouter attentivement tous les citoyens, ce qui pourrait ouvrir la voie à de nouveaux progrès.

**Résumé en une phrase** – L’abrogation de la loi anti-LGBTQ en Hongrie met fin à des années de discrimination et débloque des milliards d’euros de fonds européens, un pas important vers plus d’égalité et de coopération.
articles.personality_title_es: Hungría deroga ley anti-LGBTQ y desbloquea miles de millones en fondos de la UE
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En 2021, Hungría aprobó una ley que prohibía mostrar o promover identidades LGBTQ en escuelas y medios, alegando proteger a los niños. Esta ley generó críticas fuertes y la Unión Europea (UE) congeló miles de millones de euros en fondos para Hungría.

**Qué pasó** – El martes pasado, el parlamento húngaro votó para cancelar esta ley de 2021 y otras reglas relacionadas. Poco después, la UE anunció que liberaría 4.200 millones de euros (unos 4.600 millones de dólares) en fondos que habían estado congelados por las acciones anteriores de Hungría.

**Impacto** – Esta decisión representa un cambio importante para Hungría. Apoya los derechos LGBTQ al eliminar una ley considerada dañina y permite que Hungría participe nuevamente en programas importantes de la UE como Erasmus+ (intercambios estudiantiles) y Horizon Europe (investigación). Muestra que los líderes políticos están respondiendo a la presión pública y a las preocupaciones sobre derechos humanos.

**Próximo paso** – Los grupos que apoyan los derechos LGBTQ dicen que todavía queda trabajo por hacer, como permitir el matrimonio igualitario, derechos de adopción para parejas del mismo sexo y reconocimiento legal para personas transgénero. El nuevo primer ministro ha prometido escuchar con cuidado a todos los ciudadanos, lo que podría llevar a más avances.

**Resumen en una frase** – La derogación de la ley anti-LGBTQ en Hungría termina años de discriminación y abre el acceso a miles de millones de fondos de la UE, señalando un paso esperanzador hacia una mayor igualdad y cooperación.
